stories.headline: Pluto Security leaves stealth with $42 million to watch AI agents
stories.standfirst: Pluto Security says about 60% of the AI risks it detects come from vibe-coded tools built by non-developers, with finance staff the biggest source, TechCrunch reported.
body: Pluto Security, a startup that monitors the AI tools, agents and apps employees use at work, has come out of stealth with $42 million in funding, TechCrunch reported on 13 October. The round combines an $8.5 million seed led by TLV Partners and a $34 million Series A led by Jump Capital. No other outlet has reported the figures yet.

The company's own numbers are the most striking part, and they are Pluto's claims rather than independent findings. Chief executive and co-founder Shahar Bahat told TechCrunch that around 60% of the risks Pluto detects across its customers involve tools built by non-developers through vibe coding. Finance departments are the largest source, followed by marketing and legal. Developers rank fourth.

Bahat gave one example: a vibe-coded app built by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, which was exposed to the internet. She also said a newly announced AI tool can appear inside a company's environment within two hours of release, and that Pluto found malicious activity in every proof-of-concept deployment, some of it live attacks, according to TechCrunch.

The product watches AI tools, skills, extensions, MCP servers and the apps and agents staff build. TechCrunch says it hooks into endpoint security and device management systems, or runs its own sensors, and collects prompts, commands, running processes and permissions. Pluto says lightweight models on the device judge agent behaviour and can step in mid-task, for instance by blocking an agent that asks for permissions beyond what the user intended.

Pluto began selling in April and says it has passed $2 million in annual recurring revenue with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt and AlphaSense. It has 40 employees across the US and Israel. In April it also launched Plutonium, a free scanner for public AI skills, connectors and add-ons, which Bahat says thousands of security professionals use. TechCrunch notes it joins a crowded field that includes Zenity, AIR, InsightFinder and LayerX.

stories.headline: DeepMind details Singapore's on-device Gemma scam filter in two stages
stories.standfirst: Google DeepMind says a two-stage Gemma pipeline for Singapore scans private chats for scams on the phone, with no conversation data sent to the cloud.
body: Google DeepMind and Singapore's Government Technology Agency, GovTech, have described an on-device scam detector built on Google's lightweight Gemma models, according to a DeepMind blog post dated 14 October. DeepMind says the model runs entirely on the phone, so conversations are analysed locally rather than scanned in the cloud. No independent test of its accuracy has been published.

The post describes two stages. DeepMind says a lightweight classifier screens incoming messages first, using minimal power. A fine-tuned Gemma model then reads a larger snapshot of the conversation to confirm a threat or dismiss a false alarm. When it spots manipulative patterns, it warns the user to pause before sharing information or money.

DeepMind says the Gemma model was fine-tuned on local scam conversations, covering impersonations of public bodies and banks, and trending regional schemes. The post says fine-tuning took place in GovTech's managed Google Cloud environment, used anonymised scam reports and intelligence feeds, and excluded private or personally identifiable information. It was stress-tested on synthetic dialogues and local corpora, the post adds.

DeepMind frames the work against Singapore's scam problem. It says scams make up over half of the country's reported crimes, with losses above S$4 billion since 2019 and social engineering accounting for up to 80% of losses. It says the model was presented at Singapore International Cyber Week 2026, with a phased rollout inside applications still to be developed with the government. DeepMind gives no launch date, and does not name the apps.

stories.headline: Nvidia says RTX Spark laptops ship Friday with a 74B open model
stories.standfirst: Nvidia says its Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a 74-billion-parameter open model with training data and recipes, runs in 24GB through 2-bit quantisation on RTX Spark laptops that launch on 16 October.
body: Nvidia says RTX Spark laptops go on sale on Friday, 16 October, and that the chip inside them offers up to 128GB of unified memory and one petaflop of AI compute. In a blog post dated 13 October, the company calls it a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer in one superchip. The post names no laptop makers or prices.

The model headline is Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B, due on 15 October. Nvidia describes it as a mixture-of-experts model with 9 billion active parameters, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantisation. It says the release is fully open source, including training data, weights and recipes, and will run through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. Nobody outside Nvidia has tested those claims yet.

A first-boot screen is meant to get people running a local agent in a few clicks. Nvidia lists GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy as supported agent apps, with sandboxing from Nvidia OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers. A router library called Switchyard, which Nvidia says is open source, is meant to send queries between local and cloud models Hermes is adding it later in October.

Nvidia also says it is shipping developer plumbing. It describes PyTorch-CUDA for Windows on Arm, a native Conda installer with more than 2,000 packages, and says about 97 per cent of the top 15,000 Python wheels are ready. Llama.cpp adds decision-model support, which Nvidia claims is up to 200 times faster than traditional agents for decision steps. That figure is Nvidia's own and the post gives no method.

For creators and gamers, Nvidia cites more than 130 accelerated creative apps. It says Adobe is promising up to twice the speed in Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, though that is listed as coming soon. DLSS 5 arrives at launch, with a faster model debuting in NBA 2K27 on 16 October. Independent reviews and benchmarks of the laptops have not appeared yet.

stories.headline: Nvidia opens up the code for its Run AI GPU scheduler
stories.standfirst: Nvidia says the full Run:ai platform, which schedules and splits GPUs on Kubernetes, is now open source on GitHub, with no paid subscription needed but no Nvidia support either.
body: Nvidia says it is releasing the full Run:ai platform as open source, a day after the company's developer blog post of 13 October. The platform schedules AI workloads and shares GPUs across a Kubernetes cluster. It sits under what Nvidia calls its DSX AI Factory Platform. The code is on GitHub and a packaged version is on Nvidia's NGC catalogue.

The release is four parts that can be adopted separately, according to the post. KAI Scheduler handles GPU-aware scheduling and is Apache 2.0, and Nvidia says it also gave it to the CNCF as a Sandbox project. A GPU Fractioning Operator splits one GPU between workloads. A resource layer sets team quotas, and a Workload Map describes different AI job types.

Nvidia says it retired its own proprietary GPU-splitting code in favour of a native capability in CUDA 13.4, and that the fractions get hard memory isolation enforced by the driver. The post does not name one licence for the whole platform, saying only that source is governed by its applicable open source licences. Downloading from NGC requires accepting an Nvidia software agreement.

No paid Run:ai subscription is needed, the post says, but Nvidia enterprise support is not included. Commercial versions stay on sale through Mission Control and AI Enterprise. Eight partners are integrating it: Crusoe, Mirantis, Nebius, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Saturn Cloud, Spectro Cloud and vCluster, with Nebius offering one-click deployment.

Two related projects were named. Model Streamer loads weights into GPU memory in parallel and sits inside vLLM and SGLang while Nvidia cites Microsoft Azure results showing 3 to 6 times faster loading than the default loader. Grove, a Kubernetes interface for inference, is said to support deployments across tens of thousands of GPUs. Nvidia reports both figures and nobody else has verified them.

stories.headline: Pulse Local is a Mac budgeting app with its AI models on-device
stories.standfirst: The free Apple Silicon beta downloads about 2.9 GB of small open models and, its maker says, keeps the ledger and chat questions on the machine.
body: Pulse Local, a budgeting app for Apple Silicon Macs, is in beta and runs its chat assistant on small AI models downloaded to the user's own machine. The developer showed it on Hacker News, where the Show HN post had 54 points and 29 comments at the time of reading. Nobody else has reported on it or tested it yet, so what follows is the maker's description from its website.

The page says the app is free with every feature and needs no account. Users can pay a one-time $20, $40 or any amount they choose, and US bank sync through Plaid costs $29 a year for three institutions, with extra institutions at $8 each. Elsewhere, transactions come in by CSV import. A Windows version is planned next, and the chat answers in English only.

The models download once on first start, about 2.9 GB in total. The largest, at 2.5 GB, checks answers about money and can be turned off in settings. The page calls the models small and open and links one tuned model on Hugging Face, but does not name the others. It says the chat answers from the user's own transactions, labels what it included and checks each figure before showing it.

On privacy, the developer says the ledger, the models and the questions never leave the machine. The only regular network request, it says, checks for app updates and carries nothing about the user, and analytics and crash logs are never sent. For bank sync, it says transactions pass through the server's memory without being stored. These are the maker's claims and have not been independently checked.

The page is open about the limits. Small models are weaker than frontier ones on open-ended questions, and a money answer with the checker on takes 12 to 14 seconds. When the two readings disagree, Pulse says it is not sure, according to the page. It also says nothing in the app is financial advice, and Intel Macs are not supported.
